items.text: Does the Minister agree with Sir Geoffrey Palmer, the architect of the
Resource Management Act, when he said that her changes to the Act “will significantly
and seriously weaken the ability of the RMA to protect the natural environment and its
recreational enjoyment by all New Zealanders”?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: No, but what I do agree with Ge offrey Palmer on is his quote
where he says: “the proposals directed towards reducing and simplifying planning
documents have considerable merit. So do the proposals for a fixed time limit for the
processing of straight-forward non-notified consents, and to improve transparency
around costs and fees. … many of the [proce ss proposals] will deliver improvements to
the current processes [under the RMA] with limited impacts on environmental
protection”. I do agree with that statement.
Employment Relations—Legislative Reform and Effect on Collective Bargaining
12. DARIEN FENTON (Labour)  to the Minister of Labour: Does he believe that
collective bargaining will increase or decrease as a result of his employment law
changes in the Employment Relations Amendment Bill?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Neither.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Given that he says he will listen carefully to submissions, will he
change the legislation to strengthen collective bargaining if the evidence confirms the
advice from his own officials that under his changes fewer collective agreements will be
concluded?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: We are strengthening the colle ctive processes, and I will
be listening.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Has he seen OECD advice that th e New Zealand labour market is
one of the most deregulated labour markets in the developed worl d, with one of the
lowest rates of collective bargaining; if so, why is he proposing law that will make
collective bargaining harder than ever?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: No, I have not, but, of course, we also have a relatively
lower unemployment rate when compared with  other developed count ries as well, so it
is possible there is a connection.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Is he aware of advice from the indus trial relations centre at Victoria
University of Wellington that collective ag reements increase wages for workers on
individual agreements as well; if so, why has he put up proposals to weaken collective
bargaining, which will have a knock-on effect for all workers?
21 Aug 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 12675

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: We simply are not going to be  doing that. The fact of the
matter is that what we are doing is avoidi ng ineffective and unnecessarily protracted
collective bargaining. That is good for everyone concerned.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I move, That the
House take note of mi scellaneous business. What an Opposition in complete disarray,
from one end of this House to the other.  They are floundering. They are snappy. They
are really, really in some distress. They ar e showing signs of desperation and division,
while on this side of the House we are focuse d on what matters. I have got to say that
that is a party opposite that seems to be r un by the three “S’s”. They are making up spy
stories. They are sneaking up to meetings w ithout telling each other. They are swinging
dead fish around the Chamber. Well, frankly, th ey stink. And that is what we have seen
from the Opposition. Are they focusing on getting our finances in order?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Are they focused on building a competitive, growing
economy?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: No. Are they focusing on better public services for families?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: No. And are they focusi ng on rebuilding our economy,
providing opportunities for New Zealand fam ilies? No. And I actually see every day
that our nation’s newspapers and websites s how New Zealanders are not interested in
these distractions. They are seeing th rough the intensifying grandstanding of the
Opposition parties, and they understand how well New Zealand is doing in a world
where so many nations are str uggling. So today I am going to talk about the things that
matter to New Zealand.
One of those things that matter to Ne w Zealand is growing our debt, avoiding
international borrowing, and investing in our nation—controlling our debt, avoiding
borrowing, and investing in our nation. That is what we are going to talk about, because
this Government is focused on what is n ecessary. Every day thos e parties opposite rail
against our Government controlling our nation’s debt. They rail against our Government
controlling our nation’s debt. Ye sterday the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance,
and I announced the next stages in the float of Meridian Energy. The Mighty River
Power float has been very su ccessful for New Zealand. Almost 80,000 were first-time
shareholders. That is the largest register of shareholders on the New Zealand stock
market, a majority New Zealand ownership, an d that is despite the economic vandalism
of the parties opposite. Yesterday we announced details of our float programme.
Look, I have got to say that I think instal ment receipts are a great part of this
strategy. They are a great part  because they are going to pr ovide opportunities for more
New Zealanders to take a bigger stake in this  company if they want  to. It is pretty
orthodox. These sorts of instalment receipts have been used in the past—Westpac Trust,
Capital Properties, PGG Wright son, a number of companies. They are part of our plan
to control debt and invest in the New Z ealand economy. We will be taking that money,
including the $1.7 billion in cash that we got from the sale of 49 percent in Mighty
River Power, putting it in the Future Investment Fund, and helping build our nation with
roads, schools, and hospitals. That is $1 billion in 21 st century schools, including, as in
the announcement yesterday, $15 million into Tarawera High School in Kawerau. What
a fantastic investment by Hekia Parata, the Minister of Education.
We in this party are focused on that, and we are focused on better public services for
New Zealanders. In health we  are providing more services  for New Zealanders faster
12676 General Debate 21 Aug 2013
and with better access—providi ng the services they need. We are also focusing on that
big priority of rebuilding Christchurch. It is a huge focus for our Government, and it is a
really good example of how all our policies have been worki ng together to benefit the
people of Christchurch. The proceeds from the mixed-ownership model can be invested,
and are being invested, in rebuilding our na tion’s second-biggest city. Just look at
Christchurch Hospital—we are going to i nvest $426 million from the mixed-ownership
model. That is money that has come from—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: This Government is engaged in a
consistent attack on basic democratic rights. It is a Muldoonist-type Government, which
is something I said back in June. Since then, pretty much a week does not go by without
proving me to be right.
I think it was very useful that The Economist gave an editorial about democracy and
majoritarianism in June this year. I quote from The Economist , which said:
“Majoritarianism—the credo of an expandi ng group of elected but autocratic rulers
around the world, which holds th at electoral might always makes you right—is not true
democracy,”. It is one of the fundamental princi ples of this Government that all it needs
to do is get a single-vote majority in this House and it can ram through anything,
whether it is asset sales against the will of the vast majority, or whether it is mass
surveillance under Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB) legislation,
which the Government will be attempting to pass this afternoon. A single-vote majority
is enough for it to force that legislation through.
But majoritarianism, the idea that “elector al might makes you always right”, is not
true democracy, as The Economist pointed out. Independent courts and free media are a
critical part of that , and yet this Governme nt has consistently attacked those basic
democratic rights and freedoms. Think about  the Prime Minister’s response to the
Human Rights Commission when  the Human Rights Commissi on dared to threaten the
Government’s GCSB legislation. The Prime Mi nister threatened to cut its funding. That
is the reality of modern-day democracy in  New Zealand. The Prime Minister said: “If
you disagree with me, I’ll cut your funding.”
Think about the Henry inquiry. The Prime Mi nister’s inquiry went  after the records
of journalists’ movements in this building. The Prime Minister’s inquiry went after
Ministers’ email records, and got them. The Prime Minister’s inquiry went after
journalists’ records, and got them. This is th e kind of Government that we have. It is
engaged in consistent attacks on democratic rights and principles.
Think about the right to access the courts. In a deep democracy, a resilient
democracy, people would have the right to go to court to challenge the lawfulness of the
Government’s actions. This Government is consistently removing your right to go to
court to challenge them. If you think about the carers’ bill, that was purposely put in
place so that those people can no longer go  to the courts to challenge whether the
Government is acting in a lawful manner.  The independent judiciary has not been
abolished by John Key; he has simply made it inaccessible to the citizens so that they
can no longer get there.
The Government has done a similar thi ng with the Environmental Protection
Authority—or, really the “Environmental Pollution Authority”. It has removed the right
to access the Environment Court. Instea d, problems end up at the Environmental
Protection Authority, which simp ly rubber-stamps it all. Think about the Government’s
actions in Canterbury—and this was before  the earthquake—when it removed the right
of Cantabrians to elect their regional council . The reason it removed that right was that
the elected regional council was doing too much to protect the environment and was
21 Aug 2013 General Debate 12677
insufficiently pro-irrigation. That was the reason why John Key removed democracy for
the people in Christchurch and Canterbury.
Think about the Government’s actions in removing the right to protest at sea—the
Anadarko amendment. That was an amendment that came after Simon Bridges’ meeting
with the oil industry. That is removing people’ s right to protest at sea. Think about the
history of nuclear-free New Zealand. How did we end up with a nuclear-free New
Zealand? It was because of pe ople like that protesting at sea against the US submarines
and frigates that were visiting our count ry. The Government is consistently and
persistently attacking basic democratic rights like the right to protest.
Think about the Trans-Pacific Partnership ne gotiations. The Government is refusing
to release the text or any information about  New Zealand’s position to the New Zealand
public, even though that information is being made available to the other Governments
with which New Zealand is negotiating. Those other Governments know more about the
negotiating position of the New Zealand G overnment than New Zealand citizens
themselves.
Think about the MMP review. MMP won in  the referendum, and there was supposed
to be an independent review by an inde pendent umpire, the El ectoral Commission. The
commission came back with a series of r ecommendations. The National Party and John
Key rejected every single one of them for purely partisan, political reasons—because it
did not suit them to actually improve MMP , as was recommended by the independent
umpire.
And, of course, then we come to the GCSB  legislation. This legislation enables the
GCSB to engage in mass surveillance of New Zealanders. The Government pushed it
through under urgency, and this afternoon it will try to push it through again. This
Government has a consistent approach. It attacks democratic rights at every turn.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: When I first came into this
House, it did not surprise me that I came across robust debate and people taking
reasonably coloured positions on various issues . But I have to say that in recent weeks
and months I have been appalled by the leve l of debate and the level of deliberate
twisting and misrepresentation of what is going on in this country, merely to score
political points. Our Opposition has become so desperate and so aware of its irrelevance
and its failure to connect wi th the New Zealand public. It  knows that our agenda of
getting on and getting things done, making life better for New Zealanders, creating jobs,
and creating opportunities is talking to wh at New Zealanders want to hear. So
Opposition members come into this House, they  go to the public, they go to the media,
and they keep repeating statements that are so wrong and are designed solely for
scaremongering, simply to push their own agendas.
To hear the last speaker, Russel Norman, describe the Government Communications
and Security Bureau and Related Legislati on Bill as allowing mass surveillance is an
appalling misstatement of what the bill does. The bill is about tidyi ng up an inefficient,
inconsistent law passed by the Labour Govern ment in order to make it clear that the
way our agencies work together can continue  lawfully, as it has done for the past 10
years. We know that no more than nine New Zealanders a ye ar, on average, are
subjected to warrants that would allow their communicatio ns to be looked at. More
important, we know what it is about: it is about protecting the security of my family, the
family of everyone in this Chamber, and the family of everyone in New Zealand. I think
that New Zealanders care about the security of their country. I thi nk they know that our
agencies do a fantastic job of  supporting it, and I think th at is why you are seeing a
complete disconnect between the rhetoric being driven by a few and the reality of what
is going on.
12678 General Debate 21 Aug 2013
It is appalling to see Opposition members who simply seek to denigrate everything
and anyone who does not agree with their world view, and the last speaker’s speech was
riddled with it. How he can stand there and denigrate independent decision makers like
the Environmental Protection Authority simply because he does not like the outcome is
an appalling misuse of his position, and how dare he describe the actions of this
Government as an attack on democracy. It is our job as a democratically elected
Government to ensure that the processes de liver for New Zealanders, and when they do
not, we have a duty and an obligation to step up, and step up we do.
Let us just remember that when central governments are elected, the turnout for those
elections is more th an double, on average, the tur nout for the local body elections—
more than double. All the pow er that local government ha s devolves from central
government. We are statutorily obliged to consider and review the way that local
government performs its functions. We must, and we will, because this is a Government
that is not afraid of taking action to do what needs to be done. I have very little time for
the people who would play fast and loose with our in ternational reputation, which
underpins the security and the economic future of all New Zealanders. They would play
games with our international brand reputation me rely to score points. That is appalling.
It shows a serious lack of patriotism, in my view.
We are a Government that is about getti ng on with things. We are about delivering
jobs to New Zealanders. We are about getting rid of the wastage in the processes in our
system. I have heard the Green Party recently criticise changes to the Resource
Management Act as being just about getting quicker decisions. Well, yes, they are. I
know that the Greens have never met a process they did not want to drag out, but on our
side of the House, we do not want to see people having to spend $3,500 to get a
resource consent to remove a dangerous ch imney. That is appalling, it is unnecessary,
and we are going to change it.  I have heard every party in  this House—except possibly
the Greens—talk about the need to improve  the Resource Management Act. They
accept that it is not working well, but which one of them has ever had the fortitude to
get in and actually do it? None of them—none of them.
It is the National-led Government that is now delivering the thir d stage of Resource
Management Act reforms, which will stop hundreds of millions of dollars, year after
year after year, being wasted on lawyers, co nsultants, and planners, and will let that
money go instead to things that New Z ealanders care about—having cheaper homes,
having jobs, and having communities that work well, as well as protecting our natural
environment. That is why this Government is committed to reforming the Resource
Management Act. We are going to ensure that we get better planning outcomes. We will
continue to protect our environment.
This is the Government that cares about everything that matters to New Zealanders—
natural, social, cultural, economic, and environmental. Th at is what you will get from a
National-led Government.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: We had a rare candid moment from the
National benches when the Hon Tony Ryall wa s speaking. He told the House that the
National Government’s priority was “growing the debt”. We on this side of the House
really appreciate that level of honesty. We appreciate the National Government’s finally
coming clean and admitting that it is, in fact , the gold medallist of debt. It has borrowed
more than any Government in New Zealand hi story. It is doing it week after week after
week—billions of dollars put on the credit card for future generations to pay. I only
wish that we could look forward to that  kind of candid honesty from the National
benches when it comes to housing, because this  is an area that New Zealanders care
deeply about.
21 Aug 2013 General Debate 12679
As the New Zealand Herald commented a few days ago, the National Government’s
policy on housing is “as ill-directed as it is insipid.” That is the New Zealand Herald .
The National Government is floundering aroun d. It has no idea what to do about the
housing crisis that is afflicting our nation. First-home buyers are being locked out of the
housing market in ever-growing numbers.  Our rates of homeownership are going
through the floor. We used to pride ourse lves as a country on our rates of
homeownership, but in Auckland recently th e homeownership rate dropped below 60
percent for the first time in a century. It is a curious thing to see a Government actually
seeming to deliberately make matters worse for the people, for the community that we
are here to serve, but you can take only that  interpretation out of what is happening for
first-home buyers under this Government.
I want to make some comments about this  issue of loan-to-va lue ratio limits on
mortgage lending, or LVRs, as they are commonly called. The Reserve Bank finally
announced a few days ago that it is institut ing these so-called speed limits, which will
have the effect of putting limits on home mort gage lending. The effect of it is that 90
percent of new home mortgage lending by th e banks will be required to have a deposit
of 20 percent or more. That is a massive reduction in the size of  the home mortgage
market. It is going to mean  that first-home buyers and low-income home buyers are
going to be disadvantaged. It is  the speculators and the well -off, who can leverage their
assets, who will not be affected by this. In fact, the speculators and the well-off will be
advantaged by this policy because they are no longer going to have to compete with so
many first-home buyers.
I want to remind the House that in quest ion time the Minister of Finance, Bill
English, tried to shrug off the responsibility for this policy, when, in fact, in May the
Government had negotiated with the Re serve Bank a memorandum of understanding
giving the Reserve Bank the powers to use these so-called speed limits on home
mortgage lending. The Reserve Bank Govern or’s own words said that the bank
negotiated a memorandum of understanding to ag ree with the Government that it would
be able to use these powers and to say how those powers would be outlined. Yet we saw
the Minister of Finance shrugging off res ponsibility and saying: “No, it’s nothing to do
with the Government. It’s the independent Reserve Bank.” Well, what a load of rubbish.
This is the Government’s policy. It negotia ted an agreement with the Reserve Bank.
It is going to damage the interests of firs t-home buyers in this country, and it was only
after John Key had negotiated that memorandum of unders tanding with the Reserve
Bank that he had an afterthought and st arted publicly musing about having an
exemption for first-home buyers. Well, it is  too late. Once that memorandum was in
place, the Reserve Bank Governor did not have  to worry about that. The Reserve Bank,
understandably, is more concerned about fi nancial stability, and it is not good enough
for National Ministers to come to this Hous e and cry crocodile te ars about first-home
buyers. They handed a loaded gun to the Re serve Bank. The Reserve Bank has pulled
the trigger, and now the Government is offe ring band-aids to the first-home buyer, who
is lying on the ground bleeding.  It is offering tinkering changes to Welcome Home
Loans and KiwiSaver. It is an absolute joke.
The Government has stuffed up the manageme nt of this issue. First-home buyers are
getting it in the neck, and it is the Government that has responsibility.
This Government’s policy on housing can be  summed up by saying th at it is to trust
the market and blame the councils. It has nothing to offer Kiwi first-home buyers,
unlike Labour, which will crack down on sp eculators and build 100,000 affordable
homes.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: On Friday at 2.30 p.m. on 16 August a 6.6
magnitude earthquake struck the top of th e south, effectively under Lake Grassmere.
12680 General Debate 21 Aug 2013
This is on top of a 6.5 magnitude earthquake 3 weeks earlier, which has totally turned
the rural communities of Seddon and Ward ups ide down. I had to make a dash to
Seddon to support those who were distressed and traumatised. The emergency response
team out of Blenheim set up a welfare centre at the primary school. The Red Cross team
out of Christchurch set up a very well-equipped support tr uck. They set to work to
support those who were being affected. The Minister of Civil Defence, Nikki Kaye,
along with Gerry Brownlee, the Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, began to
make their way down to Marlborough to show their support for and their solidarity with
the people who were so gravely affected.
It was my wife’s and my own privilege to  be able to spend a night with those
affected at the welfare centre to give suppor t and comfort. It is worth bearing in mind
that the aftershocks were raining in at a trem endous rate. They were measured at forces
of between 5 and 6 magnitude and were adding to the already fearful situation. Over the
night we were well supported by the Red Cr oss. They did a wonderful job and people
took great comfort out of that. However, when we woke up in the morning, the situation
was considerably worse. Heavy rain had set in and that was adding to the difficulty of
the situation. The next morning was even more depressing than the night before,
considering the amount of shock that came with the beginning of the earthquake effects.
Large teams, however, of the civil defence volunteers reported in under the control of
the Marlborough District Counc il, under its response manage r Dean Heiford, and that
was quite heartening to see those people moving around. Mini sters Kaye and Brownlee
were also very positive and had a very uplifti ng effect on the spirit s of those who were
present. It had been announced that there would be a public meeting at the school
assembly hall and the community turned up to  hear and be reassured. We have been
well recorded with th e photographs in the Dominion Post and throughout the
Marlborough Express  showing the damage that occurred between Ward and Seddon.
The enduring memory will be of those photographs that were shown in the Dominion
Post yesterday with regard to the railway line in that area, just illustrating the force and
magnitude of that earthquake.
I would like to acknowledge the contribu tion that the Ministers have made in
assuring the community that all will be done  within the Government’s power to put
things right. That is very, very important . But, in saying that, we recognise the
limitation that will apply to that putting ri ght. You can certainly put the buildings and
the infrastructure together and make that right, but the human toll of anxiety, fear,
distress, and resulting depression will need ongoing monitoring and support.
So I would like to take the opportunity to express the community’s heartfelt thanks to
those who came along to support it during it s hour of need. The police, who got out
very, very quickly, checked all the rural roads, and all the bridges. A number of those
bridges had popped and were anything between 150 millimetres and 200 millimetres
above the road level, and needed to be corre cted so that if there was going to be any
movement it could be done safely. The ro ad between Ward and Seddon was closed. I
want to say a special thankyou to the police for letting me through at the Ward end. It
was quite an eye-opener to see the cracks and the undulations in the road as the
consequence of those shakes, and we have had many, many more since then. So thank
you to the police.
Thank you to the Red Cross for coming up from Christchurch with that well-
equipped truck, and also the Marlborough Red Cross, the civil defence volunteers who
came along with the plywood and the tarpaulins,  the fire brigades at Seddon and Ward
for the building supplies and the tarpaulins, the tradesmen, the plumbers, the carpenters,
and the electricians, and, of course, the engineers. It is good to report that the
Earthquake Commission is out on the ground at the moment, working along with the
21 Aug 2013 General Debate 12681
tradespeople. We just want to put a messa ge out and put it on record that all New
Zealand supports the efforts in Marlborough and Seddon. Thank you.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: There are two things that this Government will go
down for in recent times. There are many others to add to the list, but in the near future
one will be allowing the G overnment Communications Secu rity Bureau into Kiwis’
homes. The second, however, will be reducing the chances and the ability of Kiwis to
even have a decent home that they can either rent or own. That is a situation that has
patently become much, much worse under this Government. That will be just part of its
dark legacy. We know that homeownership in Auckland alone is now at levels below 60
percent. That is the first time ever that we have become that distan t from what used to
be a part of the Kiwi dream in New Zealand, and it is happening right now in the city in
which I live. Prices in Auckland under this  Government have gone up by 30 percent. It
is no wonder that people are finding it so difficult to get into homes.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Have you got a home yet?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: This actually is not about the ability of Kiwis to get into their
quarter acre dream. I am being asked by a member of Parliament whether I have a home
yet. Most politicians on this side know that th is debate is not just about themselves and
their own personal interest but about the ab ility of New Zealanders to own a home or
rent a home. That is something that is  becoming much more difficult under this
Government. I am appalled that the Governme nt would want us to reduce this down to
our own trivial examples in light of what other people are facing out there.
The flow-on effects of what is happening in  the market at the moment are hitting the
rental market. That is something that I wa nt to talk a little bi t about today. We are
30,000 homes short in Auckland—30,000 homes. Anyone who is trying to rent in a city
like Auckland right now knows that  that means they are faci ng higher rental prices and
frequent rental reviews, and as a consequence they are much more transient than they
have ever been.
Ultimately, that means that children living in Auckland are suffering the
consequences of our housing market. Why is that? Well, 70 percent of children in
poverty in New Zealand are living in rental properties. They are the ones who are living
in families who are paying a high proportion of  their income towards the cost of having
shelter. Even though we as a country con tinue to pour $1.2 billion into accommodation
supplements, those are essentially getting sucked up by these increases in rental prices.
The consequence is that as people get more desperate they are re nting homes that are
barely inhabitable. We are paying the pri ce of that via the hea lth of our children.
Annette King is likely to touch on this mo re, but diseases like rheumatic fever,
bronchiectasis, infectious skin diseases, and meningococcal are a ll illnesses that are
worsened by poor-quality housing.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Rheumatic fever we’re doing something about. Immunisation we’re
doing something about. Your Government did nothing.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I have mentioned rheumatic  fever, and swabbing for
rheumatic fever, Ms Barry, does not fix the pr oblem. Anyone who works in this field
knows this. Any MP who is doi ng their job, who walks around our streets, would know
this, as I found out recently in one of our poorer neighbourhoods. I saw houses that
were literally raining from the inside—such is the poor quality of the housing that some
of families are living in. If a child suffers from something like a respiratory disease, it is
ludicrous to hospitalise them for a few days and then send them back to the damp, dingy
home from which they came, when it costs ab out the same amount just  to insulate that
home as it would be to keep them in hospital.
The Government’s solution to all of this is to allow the council to bypass consent
processes, not to build affordable houses but  just to build whatever house the developer
12682 General Debate 21 Aug 2013
might want to build. The second  thing is to open up KiwiSave r a little. Eventually I am
waiting for this Government to say that the next option is for us to live in shipping
containers or zeppelins in the sky.
What we need is step change. That is why Labour is supporting building 100,000
new houses, bringing in a capital gains ta x, having a healthy home guarantee, and
ending overseas speculation. What we need for our renters, for our first-home buyers,
and for kids in this country is a vision and st ep change, and that is something that this
Government knows nothing about.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I did not want to interrupt the sp eech, and it was well handled, but I think you
may have noticed that a member shifted from  her seat and, more or less, constantly
interjected from the moment that she shifted. That is against the rules, and it seemed to
be an indication of an excessive lunch.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, there is no need to speak to the point of order. I certainly do not
agree with the member that there was cont inuous and excessive interjection. There was
certainly some interjection. This is the gene ral debate. It is a robust debate. I suspect
that although the member to whom you are referring has moved, a nd I accept she has
moved, it is possibly because she is going to make a contribution to the general debate. I
find that absolutely acceptable. [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: When the co-leader of the Green
Party spoke earlier he made reference to  the Electoral Comm ission as being the
independent umpire. It reminded me that when the commission was established in 1993,
in the lead up to MMP, that was indeed th e intention—that it would be the independent
umpire that would oversee the administration and the running of our  electoral system.
But a couple of recent incidents have demonstr ated that it has lost its way in that
respect, and it is time for reform.
Dr Norman referred to the MMP review. Wh en that review was completed and the
recommendations of the Electoral Commission were put forward, they came with a rider
from the commission that its changes were designed not so much to facilitate the
administration of the electoral system, which would have been  within its brief, but to
stop the proliferation of  small parties in Parliament. So me might argue that that is
desirable. That is a legitimate political poin t, but it is not the role of the Electoral
Commission to seek to design the electoral system in such a way that determines the
choices that voters will make. If the voter s of New Zealand want  to elect 120 small
parties to Parliament, each having one member, th at is their prerogative. It is not for the
Electoral Commission to say they cannot do it.
There were similar overtones of the Elector al Commission overstepping that brief of
being the independent umpire in the way that it handled United Future’s re-registration
process. I want to draw some of those to the attention of the H ouse this afternoon. The
most ludicrous one of all is that under the Ac t as it stands at the moment parties seeking
to register or to renew their registration have  merely to sign a statutory declaration that
they have the requisite number of current financial members. The Electoral Commission
has no power at all to verify whether that de claration is correct. It simply relies on the
word of the parties concerned. So if a party f illed in an incorrect declaration, there is no
power on the part of the comm ission to take action. But whe n, as happened in our case,
we said we were not able to comply at th at time and we needed a period of grace, the
commission simply said “We will deregister you.” So the penalty was for being honest.
When I said to the president of the commission, Justice Williams, that this was an
absurd situation and that if we had simp ly signed the declaration no one would have
21 Aug 2013 General Debate 12683
been any the wiser, he said : “But Mr Dunne, that would have been the wrong thing to
do.” I said: “Absolutely, prec isely—that is the point that I am making.” And he said:
“But you would not want to be party to a di shonest action.” The point that he failed to
get and that his commission failed to get was that the penalty for actual honesty is quite
perverse.
The second area where the commission showed  that it is completely out of touch
with contemporary reality was the matter that  I raised during question time today. Since
2002 we have had legislation in New Zealand providing for the recognition of electronic
transactions. Across a whole range of commercial and Government activities there is
now provision for the recognition of the validity  of such transactions. Indeed, at the
very height of our dispute with the Electoral Commission th e Government released its
own policy advocating greater use of electro nic technology for tr ansactions within

items.speaker: Government agencies. But the Electoral Commission said
items.text: “No, we are not interested in
that because we are not bound by the Act. We will not accept onl ine memberships as
being legitimate. You have to provide memberships signed with quill pen and on
parchment before we will accept these as being legitimate.”
The implications of that go well beyond our  particular case. They go to every
political party in this Hous e, because I have checked all their websites and every
political party in this House provides for on line memberships. Be warned that if you
ever get into a situation where you are going to be challenged by the Electoral
Commission, those memberships will count for nothing.
I was talking to a senior member of the Labour Party recently. We were just recalling
the days—and I am sure my colleague Annette King will remember—when we used to
go around and sign up member s, with a little card. Th e person who signed someone
up—if I signed Annette King up, for instan ce—would be the person who signed the
membership card. There was no requirement for her to do so, so that membership, even
then, would be invalid in the eyes of the Electoral Commission.
The point I am making is that recent events have shown that far from the claim of Dr
Norman that the Electoral Commission is an independent umpire, it  has ceased to be
that. It has actually become a rather rampan tly disturbed player in the game. Its powers
need to be curbed. The Electoral Act needs to be brought into lin e with the original
intention. I was one of those on the Justi ce and Electoral Committee way back at the
time that it was promoted. I think the Hon Murray McCully and I are two people
responsible for the Electoral Commission ever being established. We wanted it to be an
independent umpire. It is time it returned to its roots. It is time the law was updated to
make sure that common sense prevails in the way that the commission runs our electoral
system, because otherwise we will get to a point at some stage where the entire integrity
of our electoral process is questioned because of its absurd behaviour.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Yesterday I think we saw a couple of the
best own goals that this country is probably ever likely to see. One of them I saw on the
network news and was by a Peruvian soccer te am. By fate, as it were, the teams were
coloured one in red and one in blue. There wa s a cross to the midfield right in front of
the goal. The player in the red shirt, as fa te would have it, turned to his own goal and,
faced with only his own goalkeeper, kicked  it immediately into his own goal, not
realising, of course, that it wa s, in fact, his own goal and th at what he had actually done
was score a goal for the opposition. That was held up as probably one of the greatest
own goals in history.
But I think we can ask ourselves whether it really was, because, as fate would have
it, on that very same day in this very House we saw the Leader of the Opposition, one
David Shearer, kick what could be consider ed only to be an amazing own goal of his
own. That was when he stood and had a very si milar brain fade standing in front of his
12684 General Debate 21 Aug 2013
own goalmouth. He stood and confidently aske d of the Prime Minister whether he or
any of his staff had asked hi m or other members of the Labour Party to engage in
broader conversation about, or to seek s upport for, the Government Communications
Security Bureau and Related Legislation Am endment Bill. The Prime Minister, leaping
to his feet and no doubt feeling sorry for th e Opposition leader, who was standing in his
own goalmouth about to  kick his own goal, said “Do you seriously want me to answer
that question?”, or words to that effect, to which David Shearer rose back to his feet and
even more confidently asked exactly the sa me question. That question was answered by
the Prime Minister when he said “Well, actually, yes, I have done. We met after I
invited”—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s a lie. That’s a lie.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Stand up and say that. Mr Shearer himself conceded later in his
speech, actually, that that was exactly the case, because he then went on to ask about the
conversation that he denied having in the fi rst place. So, anyway, standing in front of
his own goalmouth, he asked the Prim e Minister “Have we ever had any
conversations?”. The Prime Minister said “Absolutely we did. We snuck up the stairs to
avoid your brothers in arms, Russel Norman  over there and the Green Party.” They
made their way up to the Prime Minister’s office and had a 30-minute conversation, in
which time the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Shea rer, said “Let us just keep this on the
down low, because it woul d not be a good look and I would not want you, Prime
Minister, to be shouting it ou t around the House.” Then he comes into this House and
asks the Prime Minister whether that conversation has ever occurred.
I think when it comes to own goals there ca n be no greater own goal, there can be no
greater example of brain fade, than that of that member, who would have himself be the
Prime Minister of this country but who ca nnot even recall having a conversation with
the Prime Minister about something. At least the Peruvian soccer player actually had the
dignity to publicly apologise for what he had just done and what he had got so wrong,
whereas the Leader of the Opposition, David Sh earer, went straight out on to the black
and white floor, stared down the barrel of a camera, and said “Oh, I told the Prime
Minister to keep that secret.” It is strange , that, because he was just asking a question in
the House 20 minutes earlier a bout that very same thing. If there has ever been an own
goal, that was a very good one.
While this is all going on, of course, what is this side of the House getting up to?
Well, we are doing what we were elected to do, what Kiwis placed th eir faith in us to
do, and that is to manage the Government’s finances, to ensure that we are building a
more productive and competitive economy, to deliver better public services, and to
rebuild Christchurch. We are making fantastic progress across all those scores. What we
see from the Opposition is Grant Robertson, who seems to be the tail wagging the
dog—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Worst economic record in 50 years.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Come up with a different line—c ome up with a different line. You
are going to have to renew the material, Mr Clark—you are going to have to renew the
material. Mr Robertson is all about the conspiracy theory around the Government
Communications Security Bur eau and Andrea Vance. Kiwis care not—Kiwis care not
about that. What they are seeing is the ma nufacturing sector improve. What they are
seeing is this economy growing at a faster rate than any other economy in the world.
What they are seeing is economic performance. That is what they want to see.
Meanwhile, Mr Shearer is out there. His latest is snapper. He comes in here with a bit
of show and tell—a couple of dead snapper.  Well, I have got news for Mr Shearer. He
should not be concerned about snapper, because it is not the snapper that is dead in the
water; it is that member and that member’s party—dead in the water.
21 Aug 2013 General Debate 12685

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.
During the speech from Mr Sabin, a member of the Opposition was using some terms
that clearly are unparliamentary. Can I ask that you consider asking him to withdraw
and apologise to Mr Sabin.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I know the remarks the member is referring to. On this occasion he
was not accusing anybody of being a liar; he was simply saying “That’s a lie.” It is a
robust debate. I do not think that on this occasion it was out of order.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: We have had the truth of the week
today. We have had the moment of truth t oday. In fact, we have had the quote of the
week and it came from Tony Ryall. For the members opposite who did not hear it, Tony

items.speaker: Ryall said
items.text: “We are focused on growing our debt.” That is what he said. He said: “We
are focused on growing our debt.” Yes, and he  is absolutely right. He is focused on
growing our economic debt, our social debt, and our moral debt. That is what this
Government has been doing.
Let us start with housing. What a slap in the face for New Zealanders. What a boot in
the backside for the first home owners who received this Government’s feeble, pathetic,
and belated attempts at trying to put housing policy in place. It had 5 years to look at
housing policy in New Zealand, but in th e last year it has been floundering around,
trying to find a policy. For 5 long years in G overnment, National could not give a damn
about first home owners in this country. For 5 years it was not interested in affordable
housing for New Zealanders. In fact, it was not  interested in healthy homes for low and
modest earners in this country.
We heard excuse after excuse. We were told that there is no housing crisis. Well, that
was said many times about Christchurch af ter the earthquakes—“ There is no housing
crisis.” Of course, that is ostrich-like behaviour, because now National has had to pull
its head out of the sand and admit that there is a housing crisis in Christchurch, and now
it is belatedly trying to find some ways to address it.
Then we had the Minister of Finance sa ying low interest rates mean that New
Zealanders are getting into more homes. Well,  we have fewer homes being built in this
country and fewer people getting into homes because of the so-called low interest rates.

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: That’s a lie.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Yesterday was the final insult to first home owners, Mr
Foss—and you would know a lot about it bei ng a lie. You would certainly know about
that with your background. But you would want  to know what this Government finally
did to first home owners yesterday. It is pr epared to subsidise wealthy New Zealanders
with enough spare cash to be able to buy shar es in assets that they already own, while
opposing a policy that would a ssist the building of more affordable homes in New
Zealand, under KiwiBuild.
The Government can subside the wealthy to get shares in an asset th at all of us own,
and God knows how much this subsidy is, because what did we hear today? No costings
have been done. Ministers take a Cabinet paper to Cabinet with no costings of what this
subsidy is for the wealthiest New Zealan ders who are going to buy shares. The
Government has no idea what the poor hard-working taxpayer is going to stump up with
so that some people who have got a bit of money in their pocket can buy a share, but the
Government denies that we need a policy in  this country to build more affordable
homes.
Well, it has been called the “Harvey Norman”—pay now, no interest. Of course, they
are even going to get two or three dividend payouts before they have to cough up with
all the dough for the shares th at they are getting. Well, I think I agree with Brian
Gaynor. Brian Gaynor, whom National members like to quote when it suits them, said it
12686 General Debate 21 Aug 2013
is desperate. He called it a desperate policy—buying votes. But National is not prepared
to help those buying houses.
The biggest joke of all today was hearing Tony Ryall saying that he is  on the side of
nation-building—he is on the side of nation- building. He is not on the side of building
houses. We need to build some warm, dry, affordable homes for New Zealanders. If this
Government is really interested in havi ng warm, dry, affordable homes, why not put it
in legislation that they all must be insulated and they all must have heating? Why is that
not part of its agenda? No, it is all fluff for the Government . It is all blatherskite, and
there is no substance. There are lots of pieces of paper, lots of little meetings, lots of
little committees, but when it gets down to the hard detail, Nationa l is not pr epared to
have homes built that low and modest income New Zealanders—

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: All State houses insulated unde r National—it’s called nation-
building.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: This will not worry Mr Foss, who has probably got many
homes—a millionaire. It is of no interest to hi m. All that he can do is interject. But it is
time that this Government took housing seriously, and it certainly does not.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Well, New Zealand is not at all well
served by its Opposition members. What a woeful  lot of wallies they turned out to be.
They flounder, they snap, they carp, and th ey work their way r ound the sidelines, but
they do not deal with anythi ng important. We, as a Govern ment, focus on what really
matters, which is the economy, which is families, which is housing, and which is jobs.
We are a Government that is getting on with the job, and I will give you some
examples.
We just need to look at the environmen t and conservation. The Exclusive Economic
Zone and Continental Shelf (Envi ronmental Effects) Act is a particularly fine example.
This is a piece of legislation that has been  passed. Unfortunately, of course, for 9 long
years the Labour Government, propped up by its buddies the Greens, did absolutely
nothing while 46 wells were drilled with absolutely no legislation and absolutely no
protection for the environment whatsoever . Then what did it do? It compounded the
problem. When we put through the Exclusiv e Economic Zone and Continental Shelf
(Environmental Effects) Act, which was a piece of legislation designed to fill that gap,
Labour blocked it. It tried to stop it. It argued against it. So it has absolutely no moral
high ground whatsoever around this, and I am  very, very proud that we put that
legislation through despite its pathetic opposition.
The Minister for the Environment, Amy Adams, said earlier that the quality of debate
in this House has gone downhill in the time th at she has been here, and listening to the
quality of the debate from the opposing benc hes today, I can see why she says that. But
why is that? Are the members deliberately misinformed and malevolent? Are they just
politicking? Or are they woefully ignorant?  I am tending to think with the Resource
Management Act reforms that they are absolu tely woefully ignorant. We have created a
system with the Resource Management Act reforms that creates more certainty. It is less
costly, it enables growth, and it protects core environmental standards. It is fantastic.
The Resource Management Act is A-OK. That  is what we think. The Opposition says
“Not at all.”
Opposition members are obviously not well-informed. In April Statistics New
Zealand’s Business Operations Survey cite d that the Resource Management Act led to
uncertainty, which in the past 2 years alone—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: She’s reading the research unit notes.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I am reading from the statistics. You would do well, member,
to actually inform yourself and read a bit more, because you speak constantly from a
position of ignorance. For 2 years the cancellation of projects, worth potentially $800
21 Aug 2013 General Debate 12687
million, has occurred. What was the uncertainty  that led to the cancellation of about
two-thirds of these projects put down to? The Resource Management Act and its costly,
cumbersome reforms, which do not work.
The way that the system works currently needs to be changed. A dangerous brick
chimney—one of my favourite examples—i s an $800 demolition job, basically, but
requires, in terms of its resource consents, more than $3,000 worth of costings. This is
the kind of stuff that actually has to stop. Some businesses, would you believe, have
spent up to 25 percent—a quarter—of their total expenditures on just applying for the
resource consents. The most damning of all,  I suppose, in the business survey is that
only 3 percent of businesses that were su rveyed said that the current Resource
Management Act enhanced their business. It does not work.
Our record is a proud one. When it comes to water, we introduced the National
Policy Statement for Freshwater Manageme nt. We committed $340 million to cleaning
up some of our most iconic rivers and lake s. We also introduced  a national objectives
framework. We have done more to clean up our waters to make good the problems from
past generations than Labour ever did. In fact , we have spent more than five times the
amount that the Labour Government spent, so it is simply farcical for the Greens and
Labour to assume that we are not doing the ri ght thing in this space. We are, and they
should be ashamed of themselves. They have gone a bit quiet, which is a refreshing
change.
When we look at waste management—which  is something they ought to know a lot
about because they have wasted a lot of time with their mismanagement—this
Government invested $43 million on 82 waste minimisation projects across the country
in 2009. When it comes to contaminated si tes, we have spent $5.65 million on cleaning
up those contaminated sites. Environmen tal reporting has been much improved under
this Government and under the able leadersh ip of our Minister for the Environment,
Amy Adams. When it comes to hazardous subs tances, there was no movement in this
area from that failed Labour Government a nd its buddies the fruit loop Greens. When it
comes to the compliance of hazardous substances, we have done excellent work in this
space. Thank you.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koutou e te
Whare. “100% Pure New Zealand” is a goa l worth fighting for, and I urge this
Parliament to take every opportunity to play its part in making this  real, not only in
terms of regulation but also in terms of supporting an indus try to innovate and clean up
its act. This can be done. “100% Pure New Zealand” seems to be 100 percent
ambivalent in this Parliament.
I want to address a specific opportunity to support a clean-up of a river. We have just
heard the previous speaker, Maggie Barry, sa y that it is all happe ning, but I challenge
this Parliament and every party. What about our rivers? What about  the “black drain”?
The “black drain” is a name of shame because  of this country refu sing to deal with an
issue that has been going on since 1 955. You ask the tangata whenua of the Mātaatua
waka what they think about their river bei ng called the “black drain”. Above Kawerau,
imagine a sparkling waterfall from a rive r that disappears underground for several
kilometres from Lake Tarawera and comes out at Kawerau in a sparkling waterfall. That
is as close as “100% Pure New Zealand” as we  are possibly likely to see. This beautiful
river, full of fish and life, is clean a nd oxygenated until you r each Kawerau, and below
the river it is brown. For many, many years it was black and covered in contaminated
foam, and now it is brown and still very, very dirty.
It is not the only option. We can work to wards that “100% Pure New Zealand” by
taking the modern opportunity to clean up and work with companies to use new
technology, not by allowing the courts to give  people 25-year consen ts to contaminate
12688 General Debate 21 Aug 2013
but to actually stop this kind of gross pollution. I have a bi ll, the Resource Management
(Restricted Duration of Certain Discharge and Coastal Permits) Amendment Bill, that
would do that, and I challenge the members of  this House who are in doubt about their
position on this issue to support my bill. I know that National and ACT have no
ambivalence; they are simply going to oppose it. I am calling on the other parties. Do
the right thing. Show some courage and recogni se that the people of the Bay of Plenty
and the environment of the Bay of Plenty de serve more than rhetor ic about investment
in jobs. They deserve to know that that mill will continue and that my bill will protect
them from having to clean up for another 25 ye ars, and then some. In actual fact, there
is something we can all do here—those of us with the will and the courage—to clean up
that river, so that we can make this “100% Pure New Zealand” closer to reality.
But will we? Do we have the willingness and the courage to stop gross pollution in
the 21st century, or are we going to keep going with allowing the name “black drain” to
be a shame on our national reputation? I cha llenge people to work with the mills of the
Bay of Plenty to stop the idea that they have to close. They do not have to close; they
have to modernise. They have to take t hose 25 years to invest in clean technology. We
do not hear them talking about biochar and activated charcoal. We  do not hear them
talking about modern filtration. All we hear them saying is “Do not push us. Don’t draw
a line in the sand.” Well, we are drawing a line with this bill. The Green Party is
drawing a line and saying that we know you can do better. We will work for the “100%
Pure New Zealand”. We will work with you to  do better, but we need the other people
in this House to support an opportunity to make positive change.
Our rivers are not just about a slogan and th ey are not just about visitors; they are
about a commitment to future generations, to tamariki and m okopuna. They deserve a
clean environment and rivers that sparkle a nd are full of life. Rivers are not drains. I
believe that industry in the 21 st century does want to invest in turning rivers into drains.
I believe—and that is why I have put my b ill up—that there is an  opportunity to clean
up the anomalies, to support the very few that  are still abusing and that the courts have
not addressed, by changing the exceptional circumstances clause and giving them, plus
their consent, another 5 years. That is fair, and that is reasonable. I challenge New
Zealand First and Labour, in particular, to  step up to this oppor tunity and support
industry to do its best for our environment, for the sake of everybody.
I would like to mihi to the tangata whenua  whom I have worked with for many years
on this issue. He mihi nui. Kia kaha. Although it appears that we do not have many days
left to keep this alive, I know that you are fighting hard. I know that you want this done.
I know that you are looking to this Parliament to stand up and start working—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The time for this debate has
expired.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Oh, I am sorry. I apologise. I
call the honourable member Mark Mitchell. I am excited about what is coming next,
Mark.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: I would like to talk about something
that has been in our media a lot over the la st few months, and that is our national
security. In 2006 in An Nasiriyah, Iraq, a supply convoy carrying food for coalition
troops was attacked by al-Qaeda. During the attack, al-Qaeda operatives took a satellite
phone from a dead driver. Before the accoun t was cancelled, ther e were over 200 calls
made. The calls were spread around countries like Saudi Arabia, Yemen, the UK, some
European countries, the United States, and 14 calls were made to New Zealand. Why
were terrorists who were attacking and killin g our allies in Iraq making calls to New
Zealand? That is why we have agen cies like the SIS and the Government
21 Aug 2013 General Debate 12689
Communications Security Bureau (GCSB)—s o they can find out who and why, and so
they can protect us.
Mr Shearer said yesterday that when he was the victim of a terrorist attack, he
witnessed the death, the human suffering, and the carnage that that brings. I am sure he
has played over in his mind ma ny times how that attack might  have been prevented or
stopped. The quickest way to invite a terroris t attack is to become complacent and to
say “It can’t happen to me. Why would anyone attack us?”. Is that what happened to Mr
Shearer? Was he a victim of “It can’t happ en to me.”? Had complacency crept in? Mr
Shearer indicated yesterday that he had to witness death and suffering before he became
serious about security. Well, our Prime Minister has shown that he cannot, and will not,
wait for people to die before he becomes serious about our security. He takes our
security seriously right now.
We are incredibly lucky in New Zealand that we have the most transparent and open
political system in the world, which allows  us to debate and challenge ideas and
legislation. The GCSB legislation has been a classic example of this. The legislation has
had the full blast of sunlight on  it for all to see. It has been debated until the cows come
home. It is good legislation, which has created certainty and clarity where there was
none. It provides rigorous checks and balances and multiple hoops to jump though
before any information is able to be obtained by the agencies tasked with protecting us.
Finally, I would like to share some of my own observations. I do not want to be an
alarmist but, on the other hand, I do not want a malaise to become part of our psyche—a
malaise that tells us that somehow we have  become immunised against the threats that
the global community faces. We have not. For a decade I witnessed the pain, suffering,
and fear that come with terrorism. I was fo rced to deal directly with groups like al-
Qaeda, al-Shabaab, and the Lord’s Resist ance Army. Sometimes they are brutal and
unsophisticated in the way they operate. At other times they have the use of the best and
the most sophisticated technology availabl e. Sometimes terror attacks are planned
sitting on a dirt floor in a shanty town in Mogadishu. At other times they are planned in
a penthouse in a European city. But one thing th ey have in common is a desire to defeat
security measures that Governments put in pl ace to protect their pe ople. They can sniff
out weakness and complacency at a thousand miles.
I would like to acknowledge our Prime Minist er, who is making sure that we are not
an easy target and who is ta king the steps necessary to en sure that someone like Mr
Shearer does not become a victim again. Thank you.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
BILL

sections.heading: Intelligence And Security Committee Amendment Bill

items.text: Third Readings

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That the
Government Communications Security Bureau Amendment Bill, the Inspector-General
of Intelligence and S ecurity Amendment Bill, and the Intelligence and Security
Committee Amendment Bill be now read a third time . This is essential legislation that
has attracted a lot of debate, much of it alarmi st. It is one of the strengths of our country
that people who oppose legislation have the op portunity to do so. That is their right,
whether or not they understand what the le gislation actually does. Some people are
fundamentally opposed to the work of the in telligence agencies. Those critics oppose
12690 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bills 21 Aug 2013
the agencies almost on principle. As Prime Mi nister, I am not one of those people. That
is because I have access to evidence th at shows that without the Government
Communications Security Bureau (GCSB) and the SIS, our national security would be
vulnerable. There are threats our Government  needs to protect New Zealanders from.
Those threats are real and ever-present, an d we underestimate them at our peril. New
Zealanders are entitled to expect that thei r security is something that the Government
takes seriously. We do, and we take it very se riously. But we cannot sa y that we take it
seriously and then not make the tools availabl e to allow our security services to do their
job. That is the opposite of taking security se riously, and that is something that I will
never do.
Over the past 4½ years that I have been Prime Minister, I have been briefed by
intelligence agencies on many issues, some that  have deeply concerned me. If I could
disclose some of the risks and threats from  which our security services protect us, I
think it would cut dead some of the most fanc iful claims that I have heard lately from
those who oppose this legislati on. But to disclose that wo rk publicly would in some
cases jeopardise it, and so I cannot. I can only assure New Zealanders that the GCSB is
a necessary and valuable contributor to our national security, just as my predecessor,
Helen Clark, said when she said much the same thing a couple of weeks ago.
Today, as the House debates this legislati on, I think it is important that we all know
why it is needed. It is not a revolution in the way New Zealand conducts its intelligence
operations. It is not about e xpanding the powers of  a mysterious intelligence empire. It
simply makes clear what the GCSB may and may not do, and it fixes an Act passed
under the Labour Government a decade ago that  is not, and probably never has been, fit
for purpose. So it is a great shame to see Labour now running away from sorting out the
problems it created. But here, in the National Government, I recognise the importance
of national security, and I am pleased that John Banks and Peter Dunne do too. I
acknowledge Mr Dunne and Mr Banks for their e fforts to strengthen this legislation. It
is better legislation for their input.
The legislation makes clear the GCSB’s three functions. These are information
assurance and cyber-security, foreign intelligence, and assisting other agencies. The first
of these functions allows the GCSB to he lp protect Government  organisations and
important private sector entities from cyber-attacks. This is a growing threat that targets
our information and the intellectual property of our best and brightest. Already this year
the number of logged cyber-attack incidents is larger than it was for all of last year. The
GCSB’s specialist skills can help protect departments and companies, and this
legislation gives it a clear mandate to do that. A lot has been said about this, so I want to
be clear about a few things. Firstly, cyber-secur ity is about protecting our secrets. It is
not about spying. The legislation requires the GCSB to get a warrant from the
independent Commissioner of Security Warrant s and me before it can intercept a New
Zealander’s communications. That warrant must  be issued for a pa rticular function—in
this case, cyber-security. The clear intention of the function is to protect, not to spy.
The legislation also allows for conditions to be put on warrants, and I intend to do
just that. I will not allow cyber-security warran ts in the first instance to give the GCSB
access to the content of New Zealanders’ co mmunications. There will be times when a
serious cyber-intrusion is detected against a New Zealander, and the GCSB will then
need to look at the content. That is why the legislation allows for that, but that should be
the end point, not the starting point. So I inte nd to use a two-step process for warrants,
requiring the GCSB to come back and make the case for a new warrant to access
content only where the content is relevant to a specific threat. I also expect the GCSB to
have the consent of the New Zealander involved unless ther e is a very good reason not
to.
21 Aug 2013 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bills 12691
The second function of the GCSB is, as I sa id, collecting foreign intelligence. That,
by the way, is the largest proportion of the agency’s work.
The third function allows the GCSB to assist the police, the New Zealand SIS, and
the Defence Force. This is something it has been doing for more than a decade,
including under the previous Government. At  all times the GCSB believed that it was
acting lawfully, as did the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security and successive
Prime Ministers. This is because the Government Communications Security Bureau Act
said that it could assist others, but it also stated that it could not  undertake surveillance
on New Zealanders. No agency should op erate with such an ambiguous legal
framework. The Kitteridge review identified just 88 cases of assistance over 10 years, at
an average of under nine people a year, so this is not, and never will be, about wholesale
spying on New Zealanders.
The truth is that the GCSB has unique capabilities, and it makes no sense to duplicate
those when they are so rarely used. Instea d, we will make it clear that the GCSB can
assist only those three agencies and only when they are able to show that they have the
lawful authority to undertake the surveillanc e themselves. Nothing in this legislation
allows for wholesale spying on New Zealan ders—nothing. The legislation actually
tightens—it does not widen—the existing regime.
I also want to be clear about  another issue in the legisl ation, and that is metadata.
There have been claims that this legislati on offers no protection for metadata and that it
allows for the wholesale collect ion of metadata without a warra nt. None of that is true.
Metadata is treated the same in the legisl ation as the content of a communication. So
when the GCSB wants to access metadata, it is treated with the same level of
seriousness and protection as if the GCSB  was accessing the actual content of a
communication, and there are protections around that.
The legislation is good legislation and it is necessary legislation. It fixes the
problems with the current Act and clears up the ambiguities that Labour passed into law
a decade ago. It puts in place a robust review  of the intelligence agencies in 2015 and
every 5 to 7 years thereafter. It requires more transparency through open public hearings
for the financial reviews of the intelligence agencies. It requires the GCSB to tell New
Zealanders how many times it has assisted other agencies and how many warrants and
authorisations have been issued. It gives the GCSB a set of guiding principles. It
acknowledges the importanc e of human rights, independence, integrity, and
professionalism. It puts in place a stronger oversight regime, which will go some way to
rebuilding confidence in the GCSB.
Let me finish by saying this. I have ra rely seen so much misinformation and
conspiracy about a subject as has been perpet uated about this legislation. That has some
citizens agitated and alarmed, which I regret, but my regret about this would be nothing
compared with the regret if this measur e was not passed and New Zealanders were
harmed because of the gap that currently ex ists in our security arrangements. This
legislation is being passed today because its provisions are needed today. They are
needed right now because there are threat s against us right now. Others may play
politics with the security and lives of New Zealanders, but I cannot, and will not, do so.
That is why I commend this very good legislation to the House.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I start by first thanking the Prime
Minister for coming to the House and e xplaining to us what his Government
Communications Security Bureau (GCSB) legi slation is, in fact, going to do, and may I
recommend that next time the Government puts the clauses into the bill, rather than
having to rely on a third reading.
Today we confront a challenge that count ries around the world are grappling with:
how we keep our countries safe from cyber-i ntrusion and terrorism. That threat is very
12692 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bills 21 Aug 2013
real, and I have experience d it at first hand. I absolu tely understand the critical
importance of national security, and we in the Labour Party take that very seriously. But
just as important is how we balance that w ith the need to protect  our freedoms and our
right to privacy. That is our challenge.
We are living in an age dominated by everything digital and developing at a pace
without equal in humankind. Just a few shor t years ago we communicated solely via
letters in the mail. That is a dying trade th ese days. Instead, the internet dominates our
lives, and we use it to educate ourselves and others, to create new innovations, to
communicate, and to do business at home and around the world. With it and other
technology, almost anything can be found out about anyone at the touch of a button:
where someone lives and works, what they do in their spare time, whom they talk to,
and what they say—every detail of our most private moments that we hold sacred. In
the wrong hands this technology can be used as  a weapon to pry into  our lives in a way
that we all find abhorrent. We cannot comp letely prevent that kind of abuse by
individuals and organisations with malicious intent. The po wer of the Government and
its security agencies can play their part to combat that threat , but we must have
confidence in those agencies, we must be cl ear about the limits, and we must trust the
oversight that has been given to them.
The legislation being passed today was the perfect opportun ity to be a world leader
in addressing this area. The revelations of Bradley Manning and Edward Snowden have
created global disquiet, but the sad fact about th e GCSB legislation is that all that it has
achieved is to fuel fear about the State’s ab ility to pry, not about those threats that we
may face. That has been because of the way the GCSB legislation was written and
rammed through Parliament.
We could have seized the chance to t horoughly investigate how our intelligence
sector works in an increasingly global environment. We could have robustly debated the
rights and responsibilities of the State and when and how it should deploy the tools at its
disposal for our national security. We could have based the legislation on the findings of
a full and independent inquiry. We could have  been a world leader , confronting these
dilemmas and charting through a path that w ould act as a model for other countries. We
have been a leader in the past. We led in giving women the vote in the 19 th century, and
we led in having a nuclear-free New Zealand in the 20 th century. This was our
opportunity to lead again. That would have been a great starting point for restoring
Kiwis’ confidence.
Instead, this legislation is about simply ge tting across the line. It is about finding a
quick remedy to a political hangover. John Ke y tells us that people do not care about
this issue. Well, we know th at that is not true. Thousan ds of New Zealanders have
marched in the streets and gone to rallies, and there have been debates in workplaces,
homes, and communities right across the country. They might not understand John
Key’s confused and complex ex planations about how secti ons 8A and 8C relate to
section 15 or section 14 or whatever, or the two-stage warrant process that he would be
sure to put in place as Prime Minister. Bu t they do not find this legislation at all
reassuring. They have no faith that we have got the balance right or that we have fully
thought through the consequences of this law.
Labour was open to negotiations from the beginning. We had a principled position
that we needed a thorough i nquiry right across our entire intelligence network, because
that was fundamental to getting the solution correct. John Key did us the courtesy of
listening, but he made it crystal clear that he  was not interested in any compromise. He
did not want to deal with Labour or anyone else because he already had Peter Dunne in
the bag. He had the single vote, the one vote, that he needed to pass this legislation
today. I find that deeply, deeply disappointi ng. This issue strikes at the heart of our
21 Aug 2013 GCSB & Related Legislation Amendment Bills 12693
society, our sovereignty, and our rights and freedoms as citizens of this country. It is too
important to simply bring it back to a numbers game, to a situation where you have a
willing buyer and a willing seller.
This is a sad day. We are passing legislation that is ad hoc, that is mickey mouse, and
where you have to have a thir d reading to explain exactly what it will do. It will do
nothing to reassure New Zealanders that their private lives are safe from the prying eyes
of our spies. Right up to the last minute, th e Prime Minister has been forced to clarify
what the GCSB will actually achieve, whether it will be able to read your emails, how
many warrants it needs, and what foreign pow ers it might share that information with.
New Zealanders deserve much better than that. They deserve better than bad law. They
deserve better than the loose law they are seei ng in front of us today, the law that leaves
them looking over their shoulders. New Zealan d could have led th e way in responding
to an increasingly digital age and got the balance right between keeping our citizens safe
and our personal freedoms intact.
There is hope, though. The next Government , a Labour-led Government, will take a
different path. We will act on day one in o ffice to commission the full review that we
have promised. We will seek agreement acro ss this Parliament for terms of reference.
We will involve New Zealanders at every step of the way. We will replace this law with
a world-leading one that is based on the findings of that comprehensive inquiry, because
the only way we will ever win back people’s tr ust, which has been so sadly lost right
across this country, is to get an  enduring solution that works in  the best interests of this
country. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I think I heard in that
speech a reference to a piece of  legislation that “strikes at the heart of democracy”. You
would think that if this Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB)
legislation that we are debating for th e—who knows—fifth or sixth time in this
Parliament struck at the heart of democrac y, the Leader of the Opposition could have
told us how, but he did not. In fact, he point ed out that he needed a third reading speech
from the Prime Minister to understand the legi slation and show what was in it. That is
negligent of his duty as the Leader of the Opposition because, uniquely among the
issues a Government deals with, security issu es are the ones in which the Leader of the
Opposition participates. He participates. He  is briefed, not on every issue, but on
anything that matters, actually. He  ought to know what is in this legislation before he
gets to the Prime Minister’s third read ing speech, at 4 o’clock on a Wednesday
afternoon, after 12 months of debate about this legislation.
That is what we have heard from the Opposition members. What we have heard is a
whole lot of leftover, half-w armed rhetoric about democratic rights, and none of the

have not contributed—

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: At all.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: —at all—to settling the issues that they say are so important.
That makes some of us question their intent on this piece of legislation.

items.speaker: Andrew Little

items.text: Well, the Human Rights Commi ssion did not read it, either.
